references.text: Esau's blessing also mentions the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven, but as a contrast to Jacob's blessing.
Jacob's blessing of Joseph contains similar elements about blessings from the heavens above and from the deep lying below.
Moses' blessing over Joseph refers to the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth as God's gifts.
Israel dwells in safety; the fountain of Jacob is in a land of grain and wine, and his heavens drop down dew – very close verbal parallel to Gen 27:28.
It promises blessings for obedience, including that the Lord will open his good storehouse, the heaven, to give rain and bless the work.
The Lord promises to send grain, wine, and oil (דגן ותירוש) as a blessing – the same word pair as in Gen 27:28.
It uses the image of the earth drinking rain and bearing useful crops as an analogy for receiving God's blessing.
Isaac's prophetic blessing to Jacob reflects the conditional promises about rain and harvest given in Genesis.
Both verses link God's blessing to an abundance of the earth's fruit as part of the inheritance promise.
The identical triad 'grain, wine, and oil' links Isaac's blessing directly to the covenant promises in Deuteronomy.
Both verses establish a theological connection between God's gift of rain/dew and the earth's ability to bear fruit.
Both verses confirm that God's blessing is manifested as an abundance of the earth's fruit and human labor.
Both verses emphasize that the land's fertility depends on a blessing coming down from heaven.
The psalm uses the motif of grain and wine abundance from the patriarchs' blessings to underscore God's presence as the greatest joy.
